profile.summary: 1 Thessalonians is a pastoral letter written to a very young church, formed amidst strong opposition and with incomplete teaching. Paul reacts with gratitude to realize that the faith, love and hope of the Thessalonians remain firm despite persecution. At the same time, he defends the integrity of his ministry, corrects moral and practical deviations and answers doubts about the death of believers and the return of Christ. The book shows that Christian perseverance depends not only on human effort, but on God's powerful action through the gospel, sustaining his people until the final consummation.
profile.setting: The letter is born in the context of Paul's mission in Macedonia and the brief passage through Thessalonica, a major urban, political and commercial center, with mixed population of Macedonians, Romans, Jews and other peoples. The church was planted in a trade-friendly environment, but hostile to the gospel, and soon suffered persecution after Paul's preaching in the synagogue. Most of the converts were Gentiles who left idolatry. Paul wrote of Corinth during his second missionary journey after receiving news from Timothy about the firmness of the church. The main authorship is attributed to Paul, although Silas and Timothy appear as co-remetents; their participation in the essay is possible, but cannot be defined with total certainty. The most likely date is the end of 50 AD, with some margin of uncertainty.

structure.label: Greeting and thanksgiving
structure.description: Paul begins the letter by remembering the faith, love and hope of the church and thanking God for the work already visible among the Thessalonians.

structure.label: Defense of the Apostolic Ministry
structure.description: The apostle recalls how he ministered among them with sincerity, without seeking fame or profit, and highlights his paternal concern for the church.

structure.label: Concern, sending Timothy and relief received
structure.description: Paul explains his anxiety for the church, Timothy's sending to strengthen her and the joy by receiving good news of her perseverance.

structure.label: Holiness, brotherly love and hope before death
structure.description: The letter guides holy life, diligent work and Christian comfort on those who died before Christ's return.

structure.label: Surveillance, orderly life and final exhortations
structure.description: Paul deals with the unpredictability of the Lord's day, calls the church to live in readiness and closes with instructions on leadership, discernment and community life.

themes: Powerful action of God in the gospel
Holiness of Christian life and responsibility
Hope in Christ's Return and Resurrection
Pastoral care, encouragement and community discernment
readingKeys: Notice how Paul alternates gratitude, personal defense and pastoral instruction throughout the letter.
Note the sequence faith, love and hope, which functions as the spiritual mark of the church.
Read the practical guidelines in the light of future hope: ethics, work, leadership, and discernment are shaped by the expectation of Christ's return.
profile.cautions: The introduction does not allow absolute certainty about Silas and Timothy's participation in the composition, nor about fine details of chronology, although the likely date is final of 50 AD. The letter should be read as a pastoral response to a specific community, not as an abstract treatise: corrections deal with real church problems, without authorizing speculation beyond what the text indicates.

dossier.narratedEra: The letter aims at the church of Thessalonica in the period of the Pauline mission of Acts 17:1-9, when the city was a Macedonian center under the Roman world, with a strong Jewish presence and social tensions after Paul's preaching. The narrated scenario includes the very recent formation of the church, local persecution and the public impact of the Christian proclamation (1:6-10; 2:14; 3:3-4).
dossier.compositionEra: The notes situate the essay in Corinth, during Paul's second missionary journey, after Timothy's return of Thessalonica; the date is probably placed at the end of A.D. 50, or around A.D. 51, based on the mention of Gallius in Corinth. The traditional authorship is pauline, although the notes indicate possible co-participation of Silas and Timothy in the formulation, with Paul as the main responsible for the final text.

politics.title: Thessaloniki as center favored by Rome
politics.detail: The city enjoyed the favor of Rome and the Roman citizens established there; the notes claim that it was not subject to Roman taxation, could mint its own coins and was not obliged to keep Roman troops within the walls.
politics.readingImpact: This helps to read the conflict of Acts 17 as potentially sensitive: any accusation of civil disorder could be politically dangerous to a new community.

politics.title: Multiethnic composition and local Roman elite
politics.detail: The notes mention a mixed population of Macedonians, Romans, Jews and other travelers; many Romans established in the city became wealthy benefactors.
politics.readingImpact: The church was born in a heterogeneous social environment, which illuminates both the plurality of listeners and the pressure of honor, status and employer implicit in the urban context.

politics.title: Accusation of sedition and hostile reaction of unbelieving Jews
politics.detail: According to the notes, Jews who did not accept the gospel raised up turmoil and accused Paul and Silas of disturbing the civil order, exploiting Roman intolerance to social disorder.
politics.readingImpact: Read 1 Thessalonians with this background explains why Paul insists on firmness, perseverance under opposition and integrity of his ministry.

politics.title: Pax Romana and the language of "peace and security."
politics.detail: At 5:3, the notes say that the expression "peace and security" was common in the age of the Roman pax.
politics.readingImpact: This gives rhetorical weight to Paul's warning: the public feeling of imperial stability does not prevent God's sudden judgment.

politics.title: Emerging authorities and local ecclesial government
politics.detail: The notes of 5:12-13 speak of emerging church leaders, who presided over, protected, and morally and doctrinally corrected.
politics.readingImpact: The letter not only deals with individual faith; it also shapes community life under leadership still in formation, important in a young and persecuted church.

customs.title: Ancient epistolary greeting and Christian conclusion
customs.detail: The notes observe that ancient letters began with author, recipients and greeting; in the end, Greek and Roman letters brought vows of health, and Jewish letters, blessing of peace. Paul adapts this with grace and peace at the beginning and blessing of grace at the close.
customs.readingImpact: This shows that the letter dialogues with known epistolary conventions, but it resignifies them for the Christian faith.

customs.title: Greeting with holy kiss
customs.detail: In 5:26, kissing was a common form of greeting on the face or forehead, associated with honor, friendship, and love among family members.
customs.readingImpact: The order to salute thus shows the concrete and affective dimension of Christian communion, not just a spiritual abstraction.

customs.title: Public reading of the letter in the assembly
customs.detail: The notes claim that the public reading of the Scriptures occurred in the synagogue and in the church, and that Paul's letters should be read to the whole congregation.
customs.readingImpact: The final instruction to read the letter in public indicates that 1 Thessalonians was designed for the collective formation of the church, not only for private reading.

customs.title: Work and Community discipline
customs.detail: In 4:11-12 and 5:14, the notes deal with some who refused to work and walked disorderly; others were weak or without economic and social power.
customs.readingImpact: The exhortation gains social color: the church needed work order, patience and mutual care, rather than accommodation or indifference.

customs.title: Sexual Moraisity as part of holiness
customs.detail: The notes say that some ignored Paul's teaching of sexual morality and that 4:3-8 emphasizes God's will for sanctification.
customs.readingImpact: The letter responds to concrete practices of daily life; holiness here is not only correct belief, but bodily and community behavior.

language.title: Brothers and sisters as inclusive family language
language.detail: In 1:4, notes explain that Greek adelphoi is a generic term for members of the same family, male and female.
language.readingImpact: Reading should consider that Paul speaks to the whole community as a family of God, not just men.

language.title: Triad Faith, Love and Hope
language.detail: The notes repeatedly highlight the trio faith, love and hope as the mark of the the Thessalonian church (1:3; 3:6; 5:8).
language.readingImpact: This pattern organizes the letter: the virtues are not mere moral qualities, but signs of genuine conversion and perseverance under pressure.

language.title: "Restorate" the word of the gospel
language.detail: In 1:7-8, the notes describe the faith and proclamation of the Thessalonians as something that spread throughout Macedonia and Achaia.
language.readingImpact: The image suggests public and notorious expansion, not a silent testimony; the church becomes a regional model.

language.title: Light, darkness and night as moral metaphors
language.detail: In 5:5-7, the notes explain that the children of light belong to the new arrangement of God, while darkness and night point to immoral life, moral indifference, and lack of self-control.
language.readingImpact: This guides eschatological reading: vigilance and sobriety are ethical categories, not curiosity about dates.

language.title: Armor as a moral life
language.detail: In 5:8, the notes say that breastplate and helmet are metaphors of moral life, equipped with faith, love and hope/confidence.
language.readingImpact: Military language does not describe a political war, but spiritual discipline and everyday ethics.

language.title: "Do not erase the Spirit" and the test of prophecies
language.detail: The notes link 5:19-22 to the prohibition of suffocating the action of the Spirit by rejecting prophecies, but they also require discernment to examine what is good and reject evil.
language.readingImpact: The text combines charismatic opening and doctrinal criterion; not everything that is said in the name of the Spirit should be accepted automatically.

timeline.title: Evangelization in Thessalonica during the Second Missionary Journey
timeline.detail: The notes locate the foundation of the church in Acts 17:1-9, after the passage by Philippi, Amphipolis and Apollonia, with a brief stay before the expulsion by turmoil.
timeline.readingImpact: The reading of the letter presupposes a community still very young, created under pressure and with little time of instruction.

timeline.title: Paul leaves Thessaloniki and goes to Berea, Athens and Corinth
timeline.detail: The notes claim that after the turmoil Paul and his companions left the city; he went to Berea, Athens and Corinth.
timeline.readingImpact: This explains the pastoral distance of the letter: the community was without its founders, increasing the need for epistolary encouragement.

timeline.title: Timothy is sent back to Thessalonica
timeline.detail: The notes say that Paul, distressed in Athens, sent Timothy to strengthen the church and verify his faithfulness, returning later with good news.
timeline.readingImpact: This shows that 1 Thessalonians is born of real pastoral care, not theoretical speculation.

timeline.title: Writing in Corinth after Timothy's arrival
timeline.detail: The notes situate the writing shortly after Timothy returned from Thessalonica, when Paul was in Corinth.
timeline.readingImpact: The tone of gratitude and relief of the letter becomes clearer: it responds to recent news of the church.

timeline.title: Approximate date at the end of AD 50 or about AD 51
timeline.detail: Tyndale's introduction says that the letter was probably written at the end of AD 50; Matthew Henry places her a.d. 51, relating it to the mention of Gallius in Corinth.
timeline.readingImpact: The dating helps to perceive 1 Thessalonians as one of the oldest Pauline cards, but the notes only offer approximate estimate.

timeline.title: Possible reference to Gálio's leadership in Acaia
timeline.detail: Tyndale's note mentions Gallius as proconsul of Achaia in Acaiah, during Paul's stay at Corinth.
timeline.readingImpact: This reference works as chronological support for the approximate date of the letter, without turning the date into absolute certainty.

investigation: The sources focus mainly on Atos 17-18 and 1 Thessalonians, with few notes of external context; therefore, the historical reconstruction remains selective.

There is consensus in the introductions about the setting in Thessalonica and the writing in Corinth, but the exact participation of Silas and Timothy in the composition is presented as a possibility, not as certainty.
The date is approximate (end of AD 50 / about AD 51) and depends on a chronological thread indicated by the notes, not independent proof in the letter itself.

Some social observations, such as "peace and security," "Bbeijo santo," honor of leaders and contempt for the weak, are interpretations of old terms and practices applied to the text, not exhaustive historical descriptions.
The notes do not develop in detail the economy, classes or cult of Thessalonica beyond enough for the pastoral reading of the letter; any expansion beyond this would require additional sources.
There is a clear confessional reading: the letter is used to emphasize perseverance, holiness, apostolic authority, prophetic discernment, and trust in God's faithfulness.
dossier.limits: This dossier depends strictly on the notes provided by Tyndale and Matthew Henry. Therefore, it does not include historical data not explained by these sources, nor does it reconstruct chronologies beyond what they suggest. The coverage is unequal: there is more material about persecution, eschatology, leadership, prayer and prophecy than about urban geography, civil structures or thessalonian economy in a broad sense. It is also not an independent critical investigation; when the source presents a chronological or textual connection, it was treated as explicit-source, interpretation or debated only according to the degree of affirmation in the notes. Where the text of the notes is only a devotional or pastoral inference, the item was marked as an interpretation, and not as independent historical proof.
